official_title: The Ages of Woman and Death
story_facts: Death drags off an old woman holding an hourglass and broken lance while a young woman resists; a dead child rests its hand on the lance tip | an owl at the bottom stares out at us, warning of the consequences of sin | amid a hellish landscape a tiny crucified Christ looks up to the sun breaking through clouds (Glory); companion to Harmony

pendant of The Ages of Woman and Death, same room | allegory of the innocence of the Golden Age, when people hoped for immortality through music and poetry | a serpent coiled round the laurel tree represents the ever-present threat of sin

artist: Follower of Master of Flémalle (Prado no longer gives Robert Campin)
story_facts: ATTRIBUTION NOTE: Prado labels it Follower of Master of Flémalle | the tower seen through the window is her attribute: her father Dioscorus locked her in one to stop her conversion | virtuoso flames, sparks and firelight reflections; one of the finest early Flemish interiors, much imitated; right wing of a triptych whose centre is lost

official_title: Heinrich von Werl with Saint John the Baptist
story_facts: pendant of Saint Barbara, same room | kneeling donor is the Franciscan Henricus de Werl who commissioned it in 1438 | Prado says no clear evidence Campin/Master of Flémalle or Rogier painted it, likely a follower

official_title: Triptych with Scenes from the Life of the Virgin
story_facts: ATTRIBUTION NOTE: Bouts and workshop | originally a folding triptych showing Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Adoration of the Magi; now in one modern frame | painted stone portals act as a gateway between our world and the divine | once thought early Bouts, now dated c.1465 with a second hand

Mary restored Catholicism and married Prince Philip, 11 years younger, at Winchester in July 1554 | she holds a red Tudor rose and jewelled gloves in an unusual embroidered red velvet chair | her jewel, Philip's gift, includes the Peregrina pearl, said to be found by an enslaved diver in Panama's Pearl Islands

Anthony sits absorbed in thought; devils are scattered as if preparing an assault | a fire in the chapel alludes to 'Saint Anthony's fire'; a second fire behind the tree reappeared only after restoration | panel originally arched; 19th-c corner additions made it rectangular, now covered so the arch shows again. (A separate workshop version, 'Temptations of Saint Anthony Abbot', also hangs in 056A — do not confuse)

fuses Flemish detail with Italian Renaissance architecture and ornament | oblique perspective stresses Pilate; high viewpoint puts us behind the figures below the balcony | double-headed eagle banner may recall Roman legion standards; Charity figures on the upper balcony

NOTE: the Malvagna triptych is not in the Prado; this is the Prado's Gossaert Virgin and Child | sculptural figures from his study of antique statues on a Rome trip with Philip of Burgundy | Christ steps on a book; apple = Mary as new Eve, pointing to Redemption | owned by Philip II, given to El Escorial 1572

official_title: Christ between the Virgin Mary and Saint John the Baptist
technique: Oil on paper, baltic oak planks
story_facts: alternative Gossaert | free copy of the Deesis figures from the Van Eycks' Ghent Altarpiece | Saint John differs most, with a strikingly expressive face | Gothic architecture suggests c.1510, after his return from Rome. (NB 'Virgin of Louvain' is now given to Bernard van Orley, also 057A)

official_title: Christ falls on the Way to Calvary
technique: Oil on panel transferred to canvas
story_facts: ATTRIBUTION NOTE: Raphael and workshop | made for Santa Maria dello Spasimo, Palermo, hence 'lo Spasimo di Sicilia' | the Virgin is shown suffering but conscious, not fainting, per Church doctrine | Viceroy of Sicily ceded it to Philip IV for the Alcázar chapel altar; the famous shipwreck legend is questioned by historians

Page says 'Not on display' | sitter traditionally his wife Lucrezia del Fede (married 1518), unproven | composition based on Raphael's Florentine female portraits 1504-08; early copy in Accademia Carrara, Bergamo

official_title: The Virgin and Child between Saint Matthew and an Angel
story_facts: on-display substitute for E09 | commissioned by banker Lorenzo di Bernardo Jacopi, hence Saint Matthew, ex-tax collector and patron of bankers | background shows Elisabeth and the infant Baptist fleeing the Massacre of the Innocents (Proto-Gospel of James)

technique: Oil on panel transferred to canvas
story_facts: probably for the Hercolani family's private chapel in Bologna; Vasari (1568) praised its unbelievable delicacy | Christ wears blue (sky, perfection after Resurrection) not the usual white or pink | Ludovisi collection, linked to Charles I of England (his seal on the back), reached Philip IV in 1650, Prado 1839

official_title: The Creation of Adam, Hermitage of Vera Cruz, Maderuelo (Segovia) [murals ensemble]
technique: Fresco painting on mural transferred to canvas
story_facts: murals stripped to canvas in 1947 and reconstructed in the Prado as faithfully as possible (entered 1948) | Creation of Adam pairs with Original Sin on the arches; Cain/Melchizedek and Abel offer to a Lamb in a cross | flat Romanesque outlines; painter very close to the Master of Taüll

official_title: Elephant, Hermitage of San Baudelio, Casillas de Berlanga (Soria) [murals ensemble]
technique: Fresco painting on mural transferred to canvas
story_facts: murals stripped and shipped to the USA in 1926, split among institutions; this one held by the Met 1926-57, in the Prado since 1957 as indefinite deposit from the Met | the elephant = humility/Christ; castle on its back = human suffering (Physiologus) | painted beside the Bear on a red ground; flat secular scenes

official_title: Saint Dominic presiding over an Auto-da-fe
story_facts: Dominic and six judges try Albigensian heretics | from the sacristy of Santo Tomás, Ávila; Torquemada probably shaped its inquisitorial message | some already burn; others wear the sanbenito marked 'condemned heretic'; 15th-c dress and a sleeping figure below the saint

likely Gallego's earliest surviving work, signed lower centre; donors' fashion dates it c.1470 | Pietà theme is not in the Gospels, born in 14th-c Germany | no wounds or blood and almost no gold, so the drama is Mary's embrace

from San Lorenzo, Toro, probably for the tombs of Pedro de Castilla and his wife (buried 1492) | X-ray/infrared show Christ first drawn crowned as Apocalyptic judge, changed to blessing at the patron's request | flanked by Church (laurel, chalice) and Synagogue (tablets, torn banner) with evangelist symbols

Page says 'Not on display' | one of four panels from San Lázaro altarpiece, Palencia, funded by Sancho de Castilla; State bought it for the Prado 1952 | Martha kneels reaching to Lazarus in a cemetery with ruined chapel
Page says 'Not on display' | same Palencia altarpiece | chalice on the rock = the cup of suffering; Peter, John and James asleep

the on-display Juan de Flandes panel | Holy Spirit as a dove in a great circular halo above Mary and the apostles (Acts) | one of four panels from San Lázaro, Palencia, funded by Sancho de Castilla (ex-tutor of Prince Juan); acquired 1952

painted 1573 as pair to a portrait of his fourth wife Anne of Austria | X-ray: originally a big short cape and hand on chest toward the Golden Fleece; changed to light silk cape and hand on chair arm (authority) | gold rosary = defender of the faith, alludes to the Rosary feast commemorating Lepanto

official_title: Infantas Isabel Clara Eugenia and Catalina Micaela
story_facts: court painter who portrayed the girls repeatedly from infancy; solemn distant expressions signal royal status | such portraits tracked heirs for succession/marriage: Catalina became Duchess of Savoy, Isabel Governor of the Netherlands | pose possibly inspired by Van Eyck's Arnolfini, then in Philip II's collection; the sisters share a floral wreath
